guide.summary: Kinematics describes motion without asking what causes it: position, displacement, velocity, and acceleration, in one and two dimensions. On the exam it shows up as graph reading and graph translation (slopes and areas), constant-acceleration derivations, projectile motion, and relative motion between reference frames. Almost every later unit reuses these tools.

sections.heading: Scalars, vectors, and the quantities of motion
sections.body:
A **scalar** has only magnitude (distance, speed, time, mass). A **vector** has magnitude and direction (displacement, velocity, acceleration, force). In one dimension, direction is just a sign, so you must choose a positive direction and stick to it.

- **Position** x is where the object is relative to an origin.
- **Displacement** Δx = x_f − x_i is the change in position. It can be negative.
- **Distance** is the total path length traveled. It is never negative and is at least |Δx|.
- **Average velocity** v_avg = Δx/Δt. **Average speed** = distance/Δt. They differ whenever the object turns around.
- **Acceleration** a = Δv/Δt is the rate of change of velocity. It is a vector.

The single most tested idea: **the sign of acceleration does not tell you whether the object speeds up.** An object speeds up when v and a point the same way and slows down when they point opposite ways. A car moving in the −x direction with a positive acceleration is slowing down.

Another classic: zero velocity does not mean zero acceleration. A ball tossed upward has v = 0 at the top, but its acceleration is still g = 9.8 m/s² downward the whole time it is in the air.

sections.heading: Constant acceleration: the kinematic equations
sections.body:
When acceleration is constant, three equations from the reference sheet describe the motion:

1. v = v₀ + at
2. x = x₀ + v₀t + ½at²
3. v² = v₀² + 2a(x − x₀)

A fourth, not on the sheet but always valid for constant a, is Δx = ½(v₀ + v)t: the average velocity is the average of the start and end velocities.

Strategy: list the five quantities (Δx, v₀, v, a, t), mark the three you know and the one you want, and pick the equation that leaves out the fifth.

**Worked example.** A cart rolls up a ramp at 3.0 m/s and slows at 1.5 m/s². How far up does it go before stopping? Known: v₀ = 3.0 m/s, v = 0, a = −1.5 m/s². Time is not needed, so use v² = v₀² + 2aΔx: 0 = 9.0 + 2(−1.5)Δx, so Δx = 3.0 m. It takes t = (0 − 3.0)/(−1.5) = 2.0 s to stop, and because the acceleration is constant it takes another 2.0 s to come back down, returning at 3.0 m/s.

**Functional dependence** is how the exam likes to test these equations. From v² = 2aΔx for a start from rest, stopping distance is proportional to v₀². Double the speed and the stopping distance quadruples at the same deceleration. For a drop from rest, h = ½gt², so falling time is proportional to √h: four times the height takes twice as long.

sections.heading: Motion graphs: slopes and areas
sections.body:
Graph questions are the backbone of the kinematics MCQs. Memorize the chain:

| Graph | Slope gives | Area under curve gives |
| --- | --- | --- |
| x vs. t | velocity | (nothing useful) |
| v vs. t | acceleration | displacement |
| a vs. t | (jerk, not tested) | change in velocity |

On an **x–t graph**, a straight line means constant velocity; a curve that gets steeper means speeding up; the object is at rest where the slope is zero; it reverses direction where the slope changes sign.

On a **v–t graph**, the object reverses direction where the graph **crosses** the time axis (not where it touches a peak). Area above the axis is positive displacement; area below is negative. Distance is the sum of the absolute areas.

**Worked example.** Velocity starts at +8 m/s and decreases linearly to −4 m/s at t = 6 s. Acceleration = slope = (−4 − 8)/6 = −2 m/s². The object turns around when v = 0, at t = 4 s. Area from 0 to 4 s: ½(4)(8) = 16 m. Area from 4 to 6 s: ½(2)(−4) = −4 m. Displacement = 12 m; distance = 20 m. The object is farthest in the + direction at t = 4 s.

**Translating between graphs** is a favorite FRQ task. Going from v–t to x–t: where v is positive and constant, x–t is a straight rising line; where v decreases linearly, x–t is a downward-curving parabola (concave down) whose slope matches v; where v = 0, x–t has a flat tangent (a peak or valley).

sections.heading: Free fall and projectile motion
sections.body:
Near Earth with negligible air resistance, every projectile has a = g = 9.8 m/s² downward and zero horizontal acceleration. The key move is to **split the motion into independent x and y components** that share only the time t.

- Horizontal: vₓ = v₀ cos θ stays constant; x = vₓt.
- Vertical: v_y = v₀ sin θ − gt; y = y₀ + (v₀ sin θ)t − ½gt².

Consequences the exam loves:

- A ball dropped and a ball thrown horizontally from the same height land at the same time.
- At the top of the path, v_y = 0 but vₓ is unchanged, so the speed is at its minimum, not zero (unless the launch was vertical).
- Time in the air is set by the vertical motion only.
- Over level ground, launch angles θ and 90° − θ give the same range; 45° gives the maximum.

**Worked example.** A ball is launched from level ground at 25 m/s, 53° above horizontal (sin 53° ≈ 0.8, cos 53° ≈ 0.6, as on the reference sheet). Then vₓ = 15 m/s and v_y0 = 20 m/s. Time to the top: 20/9.8 = 2.04 s. Maximum height: v_y0²/(2g) = 400/19.6 = 20.4 m. Total flight time: 4.08 s. Range: 15 × 4.08 = 61 m. Speed at the top: 15 m/s.

**Worked example (hitting a wall).** Launch at 20 m/s, 37° above horizontal, toward a wall 24 m away: vₓ = 16 m/s, v_y0 = 12 m/s. It reaches the wall at t = 24/16 = 1.5 s. Height: 12(1.5) − 4.9(1.5)² = 7.0 m. Vertical velocity then: 12 − 9.8(1.5) = −2.7 m/s, so it hits the wall on the way down.

sections.heading: Reference frames and relative motion
sections.body:
Velocity depends on the observer. If object A moves with velocity v_AG relative to the ground and observer B moves with v_BG, then A's velocity relative to B is **v_AB = v_AG − v_BG** (vector subtraction). In one dimension that is just subtraction with signs; in two dimensions, draw a right triangle.

**Worked example (boat and river).** A boat points straight across a 60 m river at 2.0 m/s relative to the water; the current is 1.5 m/s. The crossing time uses only the across-river component: 60/2.0 = 30 s. In that time the current carries the boat 1.5 × 30 = 45 m downstream. Its speed relative to the shore is √(2.0² + 1.5²) = 2.5 m/s. Notice the current does not change the crossing time; it only changes where the boat lands.

**Worked example (rain on a car window).** Rain falls straight down at 8 m/s; a car drives east at 6 m/s. Relative to the car, the rain has velocity (rain − car) = 6 m/s west and 8 m/s down, so its speed is 10 m/s and the streaks tilt toward the back of the car at tan⁻¹(6/8) = 37° from vertical.

Acceleration is the same in every inertial (non-accelerating) frame. A ball dropped inside a train moving at constant velocity falls straight down relative to the train and follows a parabola relative to the ground, but its acceleration is g in both frames.

sections.heading: How the exam asks kinematics
sections.body:
Expect three styles. **Graph translation**: you are given one of x–t, v–t, or a–t (often in words or a table) and asked about another, or about when an object turns around. **Symbolic derivation**: express a time, height, or distance in terms of given variables, then reason about how it scales. **Data analysis**: a table of position vs. time where you must recognize that x ∝ t² means constant acceleration, and that plotting x vs. t² gives a straight line with slope ½a.

For data like t = 0, 1, 2, 3 s with x = 0, 1.5, 6.0, 13.5 m, check ratios: x/t² = 1.5 m/s² every time, so x = 1.5t² and a = 3.0 m/s². This 'linearize and read the slope' habit is exactly what the Experimental Design FRQ rewards.

keyTakeaways: Slope of x–t is velocity; slope of v–t is acceleration; area under v–t is displacement; area under a–t is change in velocity.
An object speeds up when velocity and acceleration have the same sign and slows down when they are opposite.
At the top of a vertical toss v = 0 but a = g downward.
Projectile motion: independent horizontal (constant velocity) and vertical (constant acceleration g) components linked by time.
Relative velocity: v_AB = v_AG − v_BG; perpendicular components add as a right triangle.
For constant acceleration from rest, Δx ∝ t² and Δx ∝ v².
commonMistakes: Reading a v–t graph as if it were a position graph (e.g., thinking the object goes 'up a hill').
Saying the object reverses at the peak of a v–t graph instead of where v crosses zero.
Using the full launch speed for horizontal distance instead of v₀ cos θ.
Setting acceleration to zero at the top of a trajectory.
Confusing distance with displacement when the object turns around.
Adding a river current to the crossing speed when computing crossing time.
examTips: When given a table, compute differences or ratios immediately: constant Δx per Δt means constant velocity; constant x/t² means constant acceleration from rest.
In derivations, start from a reference-sheet kinematic equation and state which variable is zero (e.g., v_y = 0 at the top).
Use the reference sheet trig values (37° and 53°) to keep numbers clean on MCQs.
For 'which graph' MCQs, check signs first (is the slope positive or negative?) and then curvature.
Write the positive direction on your paper before starting any problem with up/down or left/right motion.
guide.cramSheet:
**Definitions:** Δx = x_f − x_i; v_avg = Δx/Δt; a = Δv/Δt. Distance ≥ |displacement|.

**Constant a:** v = v₀ + at | x = x₀ + v₀t + ½at² | v² = v₀² + 2aΔx | Δx = ½(v₀ + v)t.

**Graphs:** x–t slope = v. v–t slope = a, area = Δx. a–t area = Δv. Turnaround where v crosses 0.

**Speeding up:** v and a same sign. **Slowing:** opposite signs.

**Free fall:** a = 9.8 m/s² down always (even at the top). Drop from rest: h = ½gt², t ∝ √h, v = √(2gh).

**Projectile:** vₓ = v₀cos θ constant; v_y = v₀sin θ − gt. Top: v_y = 0, t_top = v₀sin θ/g, H = (v₀sin θ)²/2g. Level-ground range max at 45°; θ and 90° − θ same range.

**Relative motion:** v_AB = v_AG − v_BG. River: crossing time = width/(speed across); drift = current × time.

**Linearize:** x ∝ t² → plot x vs. t², slope = ½a.

vocab.definition: A quantity with magnitude only, such as distance, speed, time, or mass.
A quantity with both magnitude and direction, such as displacement, velocity, acceleration, or force.
The location of an object relative to a chosen origin and positive direction.
The change in position, Δx = x_f − x_i; a vector that can be negative and depends only on the start and end points.
The total length of the path traveled; a nonnegative scalar that is at least as large as the magnitude of the displacement.
Displacement divided by the time interval, Δx/Δt; equals the slope of the secant line on a position–time graph.
The velocity at a single instant; the slope of the tangent line on a position–time graph.
The magnitude of velocity; average speed is total distance divided by elapsed time.
The rate of change of velocity, a = Δv/Δt; the slope of a velocity–time graph.
Motion under the influence of gravity alone, with constant downward acceleration g = 9.8 m/s² near Earth's surface.
An object moving only under gravity after launch; its horizontal velocity is constant and its vertical motion has acceleration g downward.
The horizontal distance a projectile travels before returning to its launch height.
The coordinate system and observer from which motion is measured; velocities depend on the frame.
The velocity of an object as measured by a particular observer: v_AB = v_AG − v_BG.
A frame that is not accelerating; all inertial observers measure the same acceleration for a given object.
Motion with constant acceleration, described by the kinematic equations on the reference sheet.
Choosing graph axes (for example x vs. t²) so that a nonlinear relationship plots as a straight line whose slope has physical meaning.

practice.stem: A car moving in a straight line speeds up uniformly from 4.0 m/s to 16 m/s in 3.0 s. How far does the car travel during this time?
practice.explanation: With constant acceleration, average velocity = (4.0 + 16)/2 = 10 m/s. Distance = 10 m/s × 3.0 s = 30 m. (Check: a = 12/3 = 4 m/s², x = 4(3) + ½(4)(9) = 12 + 18 = 30 m.)

distractors.A: Uses ½at² only and forgets the initial velocity term v₀t.
distractors.C: Multiplies the change in velocity (12 m/s) by the time.
distractors.D: Multiplies the final speed by the time, as if the car moved at 16 m/s the whole time.

practice.stem: The position–time graph of an object is a straight line that starts at x = +12 m when t = 0 and slopes downward, reaching x = 0 at t = 4 s. Which statement describes the object's motion from t = 0 to t = 4 s?

choices.text: It moves in the negative direction with constant speed and zero acceleration.
It moves in the negative direction while slowing down.
It moves in the positive direction with a negative acceleration.
It is at rest because it ends at the origin.

practice.explanation: A straight-line x–t graph has constant slope, so velocity is constant: (0 − 12)/4 = −3 m/s. Constant velocity means zero acceleration, and the negative slope means motion in the negative direction.

distractors.B: Confuses a downward-sloping line with slowing down; slowing would require the slope's magnitude to decrease (a curve).
distractors.C: Treats the downward slope as acceleration rather than velocity.
distractors.D: Confuses position with velocity; reaching x = 0 says nothing about being at rest.

practice.stem: A ball is thrown straight upward. Air resistance is negligible. At the instant the ball reaches its highest point, which of the following is true?

choices.text: Its velocity is zero and its acceleration is zero.
Its velocity is 9.8 m/s downward and its acceleration is zero.
Its velocity is zero and its acceleration is 9.8 m/s² downward.
Its velocity is zero and its acceleration is changing from upward to downward.

practice.explanation: At the peak the ball is momentarily at rest, so v = 0. Gravity still acts, so the acceleration is g = 9.8 m/s² downward at every point of the flight, including the top. If acceleration were zero there, the ball would stay at the top.

distractors.A: The classic misconception that zero velocity implies zero acceleration.
distractors.D: The acceleration is always downward; it never points upward during the flight.
distractors.B: Mixes up the units and meaning of velocity and acceleration.

practice.stimulus:
A cart's velocity–time graph has two segments:

- From t = 0 to t = 4 s, the velocity increases linearly from 0 to 6 m/s.
- From t = 4 s to t = 6 s, the velocity stays constant at 6 m/s.
practice.stem: What is the cart's displacement from t = 0 to t = 6 s?
practice.explanation: Displacement is the area under the v–t graph. Triangle: ½(4 s)(6 m/s) = 12 m. Rectangle: (2 s)(6 m/s) = 12 m. Total = 24 m.

distractors.A: Counts only one of the two segments.
distractors.B: Treats the whole 6 s as a triangle: ½(6)(6) = 18 m.
distractors.D: Treats the whole 6 s as a rectangle at 6 m/s.

practice.topic: Vectors and Motion in Two Dimensions
practice.stem: A stone is thrown horizontally at 15 m/s from the edge of a cliff 20 m above level ground. Air resistance is negligible. Approximately how far from the base of the cliff does the stone land?
practice.explanation: Vertical motion sets the time: 20 = ½(9.8)t², so t = √(40/9.8) = 2.0 s. Horizontal velocity is constant, so x = (15 m/s)(2.0 s) ≈ 30 m.

distractors.A: Assumes the horizontal distance equals the drop height.
distractors.B: Drops the factor of 2: uses t = √(h/g) ≈ 1.4 s.
distractors.D: Uses t = 2h/g ≈ 4.1 s instead of taking the square root.

practice.stem: A boat crosses a river that is 60 m wide and flows east at 1.5 m/s. The boat is pointed due north and moves at 2.0 m/s relative to the water. How far east of its starting point does the boat land on the opposite bank?
practice.explanation: The northward velocity component relative to the shore is 2.0 m/s, so crossing time = 60/2.0 = 30 s. The current carries the boat east at 1.5 m/s for that time: 1.5 × 30 = 45 m.

distractors.A: Assumes pointing north means traveling north relative to the shore.
distractors.B: Uses the resultant speed 2.5 m/s for the crossing time (60/2.5 = 24 s) and then 1.5 × 24.
distractors.D: Swaps the speeds: 60/1.5 = 40 s and then multiplies by 2.0 m/s.

practice.topic: Vectors and Motion in Two Dimensions
practice.stem: From the top of a tall building, ball X is launched horizontally with speed v. At the same instant, ball Y is launched from the same point with the same speed v but at 30° above the horizontal. Air resistance is negligible. Which statement is correct?

choices.text: Both balls land at the same time because they have the same launch speed.
Ball Y lands first because it has an upward velocity component that is later reversed.
Ball X lands first, but ball Y has the larger horizontal velocity component throughout the flight.
Ball X lands first, and ball X has the larger horizontal velocity component throughout the flight.

practice.explanation: Time of flight depends only on vertical motion. X starts with zero vertical velocity; Y starts with an upward component, so Y rises first and spends more time in the air. Horizontal components stay constant: X has v, Y has v cos 30° ≈ 0.87v, so X's is larger.

distractors.A: Launch speed alone does not set flight time; the vertical component does.
distractors.C: Forgets that only part of Y's speed, v cos 30°, is horizontal.
distractors.B: An upward start delays the landing; it does not speed it up.

practice.stem: An object's velocity is +8 m/s at t = 0 and decreases linearly with time to −4 m/s at t = 6 s. What are the object's displacement and the distance it travels from t = 0 to t = 6 s?
practice.explanation: Slope = −2 m/s², so v = 0 at t = 4 s. Area from 0 to 4 s = ½(4)(8) = +16 m. Area from 4 to 6 s = ½(2)(−4) = −4 m. Displacement = 16 − 4 = 12 m; distance = 16 + 4 = 20 m.

distractors.B: Swaps the definitions of distance and displacement.
distractors.C: Ignores that the object turned around, so distance would exceed displacement.
distractors.A: Uses only the area before the turnaround as the displacement.

practice.stimulus:
A cart is released from rest at t = 0 on a track. A motion sensor records:

| t (s) | 0 | 1.0 | 2.0 | 3.0 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| x (m) | 0 | 1.5 | 6.0 | 13.5 |
practice.stem: Which of the following best describes the cart's acceleration?

choices.text: Increasing, because the distance covered each second increases

practice.explanation: x/t² = 1.5 m/s² for every row, so x = 1.5t². Comparing with x = ½at² for a start from rest gives ½a = 1.5, so a = 3.0 m/s². Distances in successive seconds (1.5, 4.5, 7.5 m) grow by a constant 3.0 m, which is the signature of constant acceleration.

distractors.A: Reads the coefficient 1.5 as the acceleration and forgets the ½.
distractors.C: Uses the distance covered in the second interval (4.5 m in 1 s).
distractors.D: Increasing distance per second shows increasing velocity, not increasing acceleration.

practice.topic: Vectors and Motion in Two Dimensions
practice.stem: A ball is kicked from level ground at 25 m/s at 53° above the horizontal. Use sin 53° ≈ 0.80 and cos 53° ≈ 0.60. Air resistance is negligible. What is the maximum height the ball reaches?
practice.explanation: Only the vertical component matters: v_y0 = 25(0.80) = 20 m/s. At the top v_y = 0, so 0 = 20² − 2(9.8)H and H = 400/19.6 ≈ 20 m.

distractors.A: Uses the horizontal component (15 m/s) instead of the vertical one.
distractors.C: Uses the full launch speed 25 m/s as if the kick were vertical.
distractors.D: Forgets the factor of 2 in v² = 2gH.

practice.stem: Ball A is released from rest at height H above the ground. At the same instant, ball B is thrown straight upward from the ground directly below A with speed v₀. Air resistance is negligible. For what value of v₀ do the balls collide at the instant ball B reaches its highest point?
practice.explanation: Both balls have the same acceleration g, so relative to each other they move at constant speed v₀ and close the gap H in t = H/v₀. Ball B peaks at t = v₀/g. Setting H/v₀ = v₀/g gives v₀² = gH, so v₀ = √(gH). Check: at that time A has fallen ½g(H/v₀)² = H/2 and B has risen v₀²/2g = H/2, so they meet at mid-height.

distractors.C: Requires B to reach height H at its peak, ignoring that A also falls.
distractors.D: Doubles the correct answer, usually from using t = 2v₀/g (total flight time) for the peak.
distractors.B: Sets B's peak height (v₀²/2g) equal to H/4 or mishandles the meeting time.

practice.topic: Vectors and Motion in Two Dimensions
practice.stem: A ball is launched from ground level at 20 m/s at 37° above the horizontal toward a vertical wall 24 m away. Use sin 37° ≈ 0.60 and cos 37° ≈ 0.80. Air resistance is negligible. Where does the ball hit the wall, and what is its vertical motion at that instant?

choices.text: About 7.0 m above the ground, moving downward
About 7.0 m above the ground, moving upward
About 18 m above the ground, moving upward
About 11 m above the ground, moving downward

practice.explanation: vₓ = 16 m/s, v_y0 = 12 m/s. Time to reach the wall: 24/16 = 1.5 s. Height: 12(1.5) − ½(9.8)(1.5)² = 18 − 11.0 = 7.0 m. Vertical velocity: 12 − 9.8(1.5) = −2.7 m/s, so the ball is already descending (its peak was at t = 1.22 s).

distractors.C: Forgets the −½gt² term (18 m is just v_y0·t).
distractors.D: Uses the wrong time or swaps sine and cosine in the components.
distractors.B: Gets the height right but does not check the sign of v_y; the peak occurred before 1.5 s.

practice.stem: On a windless day, raindrops fall vertically at a constant 8.0 m/s relative to the ground. A car drives east at a constant 6.0 m/s. As seen by a passenger in the car, which describes the raindrops' motion?

choices.text: Speed 8.0 m/s, falling vertically, because the car's horizontal motion does not affect vertical motion
Speed 10 m/s, slanting downward and toward the front of the car (eastward), 37° from vertical
Speed 14 m/s, slanting downward and toward the back of the car, 53° from vertical
Speed 10 m/s, slanting downward and toward the back of the car (westward), 37° from vertical

practice.explanation: v_rain,car = v_rain,ground − v_car,ground = (0, −8) − (6, 0) = (−6 m/s east, −8 m/s up), i.e., 6 m/s west and 8 m/s down. Magnitude √(36 + 64) = 10 m/s; angle from vertical tan⁻¹(6/8) = 37°, tilted toward the rear.

distractors.B: Adds the car's velocity instead of subtracting it.
distractors.C: Adds magnitudes (6 + 8) and measures the angle from the wrong axis.
distractors.A: Correct that vertical motion is unaffected, but horizontal relative motion still exists.

practice.stimulus:
An object moving along the x-axis has velocity −2.0 m/s at t = 0. Its acceleration is:

| Time interval | Acceleration |
| --- | --- |
| 0 to 3.0 s | +2.0 m/s² |
| 3.0 s to 5.0 s | −3.0 m/s² |
practice.stem: What are the object's velocity at t = 5.0 s and its displacement from t = 0 to t = 5.0 s?
practice.explanation: 0–3 s: v(3) = −2 + 2(3) = +4 m/s; Δx₁ = (−2)(3) + ½(2)(9) = +3 m. 3–5 s: v(5) = 4 − 3(2) = −2 m/s; Δx₂ = 4(2) − ½(3)(4) = +2 m. Total Δx = +5 m. The final velocity happens to equal the initial velocity because the total area under a–t is 6 − 6 = 0.

distractors.A: Reasons that equal start and end velocities mean constant velocity, then uses Δx = (−2)(5).
distractors.C: Stops at the velocity reached at t = 3 s.
distractors.D: Drops the sign of the second acceleration in one of the steps.

practice.prompt: A cart on a long horizontal track has a fan attached that exerts a constant force, giving the cart a constant acceleration of magnitude a directed in the −x direction. At t = 0 the cart is at x = 0 and moving in the +x direction with speed v₀. Friction is negligible.

parts.label: A
parts.prompt: Derive an expression for the maximum position x_max the cart reaches, in terms of v₀, a, and physical constants as appropriate. Begin your derivation by writing a fundamental physics principle or an equation from the reference information.

parts.label: B
parts.prompt: Describe a sketch of the cart's velocity v as a function of time t from t = 0 until the cart returns to x = 0. Label the time at which v = 0 and the velocity at the instant the cart returns to x = 0.

parts.label: C
parts.prompt: In one trial, v₀ = 1.2 m/s and a = 0.40 m/s². Calculate x_max and the time at which the cart returns to x = 0.

parts.label: D
parts.prompt: A student claims: 'If the initial speed is doubled with the same fan setting, the cart will go twice as far before turning around.' Indicate whether the claim is correct, and justify your answer using your expression from part A.

rubric.description: Writes a kinematic equation from the reference sheet relating velocity, acceleration, and displacement, e.g., v² = v₀² + 2a(x − x₀).
Substitutes v = 0 at the turnaround and uses −a for the acceleration (or equivalent sign handling).
Straight line with constant negative slope starting at +v₀ at t = 0 and crossing zero at t = v₀/a.
Line ends at v = −v₀ at t = 2v₀/a (the equal-areas condition for returning to x = 0).
States that x_max is proportional to v₀² (from part A).
Concludes that doubling v₀ makes x_max four times as large, consistent with the expression.

practice.sampleResponse:
**A.** v² = v₀² + 2a(x − x₀). At the turnaround v = 0, x₀ = 0, and the acceleration is −a: 0 = v₀² − 2a·x_max, so **x_max = v₀²/(2a)**.

**B.** The graph is a single straight line with negative slope −a. It starts at v = +v₀ at t = 0, crosses v = 0 at t = v₀/a (the turnaround), and continues to v = −v₀ at t = 2v₀/a, when the cart is back at x = 0 (the positive area before the crossing equals the negative area after it).

**C.** x_max = (1.2 m/s)²/(2 × 0.40 m/s²) = **1.8 m**. Return time t = 2v₀/a = 2(1.2)/0.40 = **6.0 s**.

**D.** The claim is incorrect. From part A, x_max = v₀²/(2a), so x_max is proportional to the square of the initial speed when a is unchanged. Doubling v₀ multiplies x_max by 2² = 4, so the cart goes four times as far, not twice as far.
